name: Reconnaissance
description:
The fraud actor's actions to gather information they can use to plan future operations, including both cyber intrusions and attempted fraud. 

Reconnaissance consists of techniques that involve fraud actors actively or passively gathering information that can be used to support targeting. Such information may include details of the victim organization, infrastructure, or staff/personnel. This information can be leveraged by the fraud actor to aid in other phases of the fraud lifecycle, such as using gathered information to plan and execute Initial Access, to scope and prioritize post-compromise objectives, or to drive and lead further Reconnaissance efforts.

name: Resource Development
description:
The fraud actor's actions to establish resources they can use to support both cyber and fraud activities. 

Resource Development consists of techniques that involve fraud actors creating, purchasing, or compromising/stealing resources that can be used to support targeting. Such resources include infrastructure, accounts, or capabilities. These resources can be leveraged by the fraud actor to aid in other phases of the fraud lifecycle, such as using purchased domains to support Execution, email accounts for phishing as a part of Initial Access, or spoofing to help with Stealth.

name: Initial Access
description:
The fraud actor's actions to gain a foothold in a selected environment.  

Initial Access consists of techniques that use various entry vectors to gain their initial foothold within a selected environment. Techniques used to gain a foothold include targeted spearphishing and exploiting weaknesses in browsers. Footholds gained through initial access may allow for continued access, like compromise accounts and use of external remote services, or may be limited-use due to changing passwords.

name: Stealth
description:
The fraud actor is trying to hide and conceal fraudulent activity by appearing as normal user or business behavior.

Stealth consists of techniques that reduce the likelihood of detection by blending in with legitimate activity or minimizing observable indicators of fraud. These techniques are characterized by concealment behaviors such as obfuscation, impersonation, traffic shaping, or mimicking normal customer operations, without directly modifying security controls or monitoring systems. The goal is to remain indistinguishable from benign activity while leaving defensive systems operational and intact.

name: Defense Impairment
description:
The fraud actor is trying to break or undermine security mechanisms, fraud controls, or customer safeguards, so defenders or victims cannot respond to fraudulent activity.

Defense Impairment consists of techniques that degrade, disable, evade, or undermine the effectiveness and trustworthiness of security controls, fraud prevention systems, and customer-facing security features. This is characterized by direct interference with defensive technologies, operational processes, or user security controls. This may include disabling account alerts, suppressing notifications, modifying contact information, or bypassing authentication safeguards. The goal is to reduce the ability of organizations and victims to identify, prevent, or respond to fraud activity.

name: Positioning
description:
The fraud actor's actions in a selected environment, after initial access, to collect or manipulate data or otherwise prepare for execution. 
                   
Positioning consists of techniques that involve fraud actors gathering sensitive information, altering account configurations, manipulating transaction parameters, or establishing conditions necessary for successful fraud operations. These preparatory activities enable fraud actors to maximize the value extracted during fraud execution or establish persistent access for future operations.

name: Execution
description:
The fraud actor's actions to run malicious code or initiate fraudulent transactions that will convert stolen data to money. 

Execution consists of techniques that result in fraud actor‑controlled code or actions running on a local, remote, or transaction‑processing system. Techniques that run malicious code or automate actions are often paired with other tactics to achieve broader goals, such as exploring a network, manipulating applications, initiating unauthorized payments, or altering transaction data to support fraud. For example, a fraud actor might use a remote access tool to run a PowerShell script that performs Remote System Discovery and then launch scripts or bots that submit fraudulent transfers, modify payment instructions, or replay payment messages through compromised banking or merchant platforms.

name: Monetization
description:
The fraud actor's actions to convert assets, often stolen, into usable funds or value in their possession.

Fraud actors may convert fraudulently obtained funds or assets into a form they can utilize or transfer to their possession. Monetization consists of techniques that involve fraud actors liquidating stolen digital assets, transferring funds from compromised accounts, converting fraud proceeds into difficult-to-trace monetary instruments, or manipulating markets. These techniques represent the final stages of fraud operations where fraud actors secure their gains and attempt to obscure the transaction trail.

name: 3DS Bypass
description: Fraud actors may exploit weaknesses in 3-D Secure authentication implementations to bypass additional security verification for card-not-present transactions. This may include deliberately providing incomplete cardholder information to cause authentication failures that result in transactions being processed without additional verification. Bypassing 3DS authentication allows fraud actors to conduct fraudulent transactions without completing the additional security challenges designed to prevent card-not-present fraud.

name: Abuse of Public-Facing API
description: Fraud actors may exploit publicly available APIs intended for legitimate customer or partner use to facilitate fraud operations. This may include account enumeration, credential stuffing attacks, data scraping, or automated financial transaction fraud. Fraud actors often leverage compromised credentials, botnets, or custom scripts to generate high volumes of API requests that mimic legitimate traffic patterns.

name: Abuse of Public-Facing API: Mobile API Abuse
description: Fraud actors may exploit mobile-specific APIs to conduct fraud operations. This may include using modified mobile applications, mobile device emulators, or custom scripts to generate fraudulent API calls that appear legitimate. Fraud actors target mobile APIs to bypass security controls designed for web-based access or to exploit mobile-specific vulnerabilities in authentication and authorization mechanisms.

name: Abuse of Public-Facing API: Web API Abuse
description: Fraud actors may abuse web-based APIs exposed through websites or web applications to automate fraud operations. This may include leveraging botnets, proxy networks, or headless browsers to mimic legitimate web traffic while conducting credential stuffing, transaction fraud, or data exfiltration. Fraud actors exploit web APIs to bypass rate limiting, CAPTCHA controls, or other security mechanisms designed to prevent automated abuse.

name: Abuse SMS verification
description:
Fraud actors may abuse SMS verification and one-time-password (OTP) services to generate excessive messaging costs or facilitate toll‑fraud schemes, rather than to authenticate real users. In a common pattern, attackers script large numbers of account sign‑ups or login attempts that all trigger SMS verifications to premium‑rate or otherwise high‑tariff phone numbers they control, allowing them to collect a share of the inflated termination fees while the victim organization pays the messaging bill. 

Adversaries may also manipulate SMS routing by steering verification traffic through specific high‑cost international carriers or number ranges, disguising these as normal mobile destinations so that automated routing systems deliver the messages without suspicion. By driving sustained volumes of verification traffic into these expensive routes, attackers can rapidly increase the victim’s telecom spend and monetize the difference between actual delivery cost and what the organization expects to pay for legitimate verification usage. 

This technique focuses on cost and routing abuse of SMS verification itself, and is distinct from Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation, which covers triggering MFA prompts or notifications to overwhelm or pressure victims into approving authentication attempts.

name: Access with Stolen Session Cookie
description: Fraud actors may use stolen session cookies to gain unauthorized access to user accounts without requiring authentication credentials. Session cookies maintain user login state and may be obtained through phishing, malware, network interception, or data breaches. By replaying stolen session cookies, fraud actors can impersonate legitimate users and access accounts as long as the session remains valid.

name: Account Manipulation
description: Fraud actors may modify account settings to facilitate fraud operations or maintain persistent access. This may include altering payment methods, changing contact information, modifying notification preferences, adjusting security settings, linking accounts, or adding users. Fraud actors typically gain initial access through stolen credentials or system vulnerabilities, then make unauthorized changes to account configurations to support subsequent fraud activities or prevent detection.

name: Account Manipulation: Account Linking
description: Fraud actors may link compromised accounts to accounts under their control to establish persistent access that survives credential resets. In online and mobile banking environments, fraud actors may link victim bank accounts to secondary credentials or profiles without the victim's knowledge. This technique allows fraud actors to maintain account access even after the victim changes primary authentication credentials.

name: Account Manipulation: Add Authorized User
description: Fraud actors may add themselves or accomplices as authorized users or secondary signers on compromised accounts. Authorized users typically have permission to perform transactions and access account features on behalf of the primary account holder. This technique provides fraud actors with legitimate-appearing access to accounts and may be used to position access for monetization or to establish persistent access that appears authorized.

name: Account Manipulation: Add Beneficiary
description: Fraud actors may add themselves or accounts under their control as beneficiaries on compromised financial accounts. Beneficiary designations determine who receives account assets or benefits after the account holder's death or under other specified conditions. This technique allows fraud actors to potentially receive account assets in the future or to establish fraudulent claims to account benefits.

name: Account Manipulation: Change Account Details
description: Fraud actors may change account details such as PINs, security questions, transaction limits, addresses, phone numbers, email address, or other account parameters. By modifying these details, fraud actors can reduce security controls, increase their operational capabilities, or prevent legitimate users from accessing or recovering accounts. This may include changing knowledge-based authentication answers or adjusting account restrictions.

name: Account Manipulation: Change E-Delivery or Notification Settings
description: Fraud actors may change electronic delivery or notification settings to prevent account holders from detecting suspicious account activity. By disabling email alerts, SMS notifications, or other notification mechanisms, fraud actors can conduct fraudulent transactions or account modifications without triggering alerts that would otherwise notify the legitimate account owner.

name: Account Manipulation: Change of Payment Details
description: Fraud actors may alter stored payment or payout details in compromised customer, merchant, or vendor accounts to redirect non‑payroll funds to accounts or instruments they control. This can include changing bank information for vendor payments or customer refunds, updating stored cards or digital wallets used for billing, or adding new payment methods to enable unauthorized purchases and withdrawals, while leaving payroll processes untouched.

name: Account Manipulation: Enable Account Features
description: Fraud actors may enable additional account features that legitimate account holders did not intend to activate. This may include increasing transaction limits, enabling international transactions, activating overdraft protection, or enabling other features that facilitate unauthorized financial activities. By expanding account capabilities, fraud actors increase their ability to monetize compromised accounts.

name: Account Manipulation: Update Call Receiving Device
description: Fraud actors may add devices under their control to victim accounts to intercept phone calls intended for the legitimate account holder. This may include adding devices to cloud account profiles such as Apple ID or Microsoft accounts. By intercepting phone calls, fraud actors can receive authentication codes sent via voice calls, intercept customer service callbacks, or monitor communication related to account security.

name: Account Takeover
description:
Fraud actors may gain unauthorized access and control of a customer’s bank or payment account on a financial platform or service. This typically involves compromising the account used to hold and move funds—such as online banking, card‑issuing, or digital wallet accounts—rather than general user or application accounts covered under Compromise Accounts.

Fraud actors may achieve bank account takeover by using stolen credentials, exploiting system vulnerabilities, conducting phishing attacks, bypassing MFA, or leveraging credential stuffing with previously breached credentials. Once access is obtained, they can change contact and security details, add or modify payees, redirect deposits or payouts, initiate unauthorized transfers and card‑not‑present transactions, or extract sensitive financial data that supports additional fraud against the customer or institution.

name: Account Takeover: Exposed API Key
description:
Fraudsters may take over accounts by obtaining exposed API keys that are intended to authorize programmatic access to financial services. An exposed key can allow unauthorized interaction with payment platforms, enabling access to account data, manipulation of payment flows, and initiation of illicit transactions without traditional interactive login.

API keys may be exposed through insecure code repositories, plaintext configuration files, shared code snippets, or targeted phishing of developers and technical staff. Once obtained, fraudsters can use the key to retrieve transaction and customer information, create or modify transactions and refunds for their own benefit, alter payment configuration to reroute future funds, or harvest data that supports follow‑on phishing or fraud campaigns.

name: Account Takeover: Exposed Login Credential
description:
Fraudsters may gain control of accounts by using exposed passkeys or login credentials, such as usernames and passwords leaked or stolen from other sources. Using these credentials, they authenticate directly to payment or account portals and assume the identity of the legitimate user, often without triggering additional verification if passwords are reused or multifactor controls are weak.

Login credentials can be obtained via large‑scale data breaches, credential‑stuffing lists, phishing campaigns, or keylogging malware. After gaining access, fraudsters may change routing details or payout instructions, initiate withdrawals or refunds, view and exfiltrate sensitive customer data, adjust billing or invoicing settings to redirect future payments, or use the compromised account as infrastructure for additional fraud schemes.

name: Account Takeover: Password Reset
description: Fraudsters may seize control of accounts by abusing password reset and account recovery mechanisms. By compromising a victim’s email account or intercepting reset links and one‑time codes, they can initiate and complete password reset flows without the legitimate user’s knowledge. Once the reset is successful, fraudsters establish new credentials under their control, lock the victim out of the account, and can freely modify settings, payment details, or perform unauthorized transactions.

name: Adversary-in-the-Browser
description: Fraud actors may use malware or malicious browser components to intercept, monitor, or manipulate web browser activity and transactions. This may include injecting malicious code into browser processes, deploying malicious browser extensions, or using DLL injection to compromise browser operations. Adversary-in-the-browser techniques allow real-time interception and modification of web traffic, including credential capture and transaction manipulation.

name: Adversary-in-the-Browser: DLL Injection
description: Fraud actors may inject malicious dynamic-link libraries into legitimate browser processes to intercept and manipulate web traffic. Injected DLLs can capture credentials, modify displayed content, intercept form data, or manipulate financial transactions in real-time. This technique allows fraud actors to bypass browser security controls and operate within the context of trusted browser processes.

name: Adversary-in-the-Browser: Malicious Browser Extension
description: Fraud actors may deploy malicious browser extensions that appear legitimate but contain hidden functionality to steal credentials or intercept financial transactions. Malicious extensions can monitor web activity, capture form inputs including payment information, modify displayed content, or inject malicious scripts into visited web pages. Users may be deceived into installing these extensions through social engineering or by compromising legitimate extension distribution channels.

name: Adversary-in-the-Browser: Malicious JavaScript Injection
description: Fraud actors may inject malicious JavaScript into legitimate web pages to intercept credentials, capture payment information, or manipulate financial transactions. This may be accomplished through compromising web servers, exploiting cross-site scripting vulnerabilities, or using browser-based malware to modify page content before rendering. Injected JavaScript operates within the security context of the legitimate website, making detection more difficult.

name: ATM Manipulation
description: Fraud actors may manipulate ATM hardware or software to steal financial data or dispense unauthorized cash. This may include installing malicious software, exploiting vulnerabilities, connecting unauthorized hardware devices, or physically manipulating ATM components. ATM manipulation techniques allow fraud actors to capture card data and PINs, dispense cash without proper authorization, or disable security controls.

name: ATM Manipulation: ATM Hardware Manipulation
description: Fraud actors may manipulate ATM hardware to gain unauthorized access or control. This may include installing black box devices that connect to internal ATM systems, modifying card readers to capture card data, or physically accessing internal communication interfaces. Hardware manipulation techniques such as ATM black boxing involve connecting unauthorized devices to the ATM's internal systems to send fraudulent dispense commands.

name: ATM Manipulation: ATM Software Manipulation
description: Fraud actors may manipulate ATM software to gain unauthorized access to sensitive financial data or conduct unauthorized transactions. This may include installing malicious software, exploiting software vulnerabilities, or modifying ATM operating system configurations. Software manipulation can allow fraud actors to capture card data and PINs, dispense cash without authorization, or disable security controls.

name: Bank Deposit
description: Fraud actors may exploit bank deposit mechanisms to introduce fraudulent funds, kite checks, or launder money. This may include depositing counterfeit checks, manipulating mobile deposit systems, exploiting deposit timing vulnerabilities, or using stolen instruments. Bank deposit fraud techniques exploit the delay between deposit and verification or clearing of deposited instruments.

name: Bank Deposit: ATM Deposit
description: Fraud actors may exploit ATM deposit functions to introduce fraudulent checks or cash into accounts. This may include depositing counterfeit checks, altered checks, or stolen instruments through ATMs that process deposits with limited immediate verification. ATM deposits may provide longer processing times before fraud is detected compared to teller deposits.

name: Bank Deposit: Mobile Deposit
description: Fraud actors may exploit mobile deposit capabilities to deposit fraudulent checks or repeatedly deposit the same check. This may include depositing counterfeit checks, altered checks, or exploiting check processing delays to deposit the same check through multiple channels before fraud is detected. Mobile deposit systems may have reduced verification compared to in-person deposits.

name: Bank Deposit: Night Deposit
description: Fraud actors may exploit night deposit services to introduce fraudulent deposits with delayed verification. Night deposits are processed the following business day, providing additional time for fraud actors to exploit the float period before deposits are verified. This may include depositing counterfeit checks, stolen checks, or altered instruments.

name: Bank Deposit: Test Deposit
description: Fraud actors may abuse test deposit mechanisms used for account verification to gather account information or conduct micro-deposit fraud. Account linking services often send small test deposits that users must verify, and fraud actors may intercept these deposits to confirm account control or conduct account enumeration. This technique may also be used to identify active accounts for targeting.

name: Card Dump Capture
description: Fraud actors may capture payment card magnetic stripe data, EMV chip data, or card details from various sources. This may include using skimming devices at point-of-sale terminals, ATMs, or fuel pumps, compromising payment processing systems, or conducting memory scraping attacks against POS systems. Captured card data can be used to create counterfeit cards, conduct card-not-present fraud, or be sold to other malicious fraud actors.

name: Card Testing
description: Fraud actors may test stolen payment card credentials by conducting small transactions to determine if cards are valid and active. This may include making small purchases, authorization attempts without completing transactions, or using automated testing services. Successful card tests confirm which stolen credentials remain valid for use in larger fraudulent transactions or for sale to other malicious fraud actors.

name: Change Payroll Details
description: Fraud actors may alter payroll or HR system settings so that an employee’s salary or wage payments are redirected to accounts they control. This typically involves changing direct‑deposit account and routing numbers, updating payee details, or modifying payroll profiles inside dedicated payroll/HR platforms, resulting in ongoing diversion of regular paycheck deposits away from the legitimate employee.

name: Check Fraud
description: Fraud Actors may illicitly obtain funds by abusing paper or digital checks tied to existing accounts. This can involve stealing checks, forging signatures or endorsements, issuing counterfeit or unauthorized checks, altering payee or amount details, or “washing” and reusing legitimate checks, all with the goal of cashing out or redirecting funds without the account holder’s consent.

name: Churning
description:
Churning fraud occurs when fraud actors repeatedly use stolen payment card information to conduct transactions until the card limit is reached or the account balance is depleted, often before detection or card deactivation.

Fraud actors typically begin with a low‑value test transaction to confirm that the card details are valid and active, then rapidly execute a series of higher‑value transactions. These transactions often involve card‑not‑present channels such as eCommerce, digital goods and services, or purchases that can be quickly resold, including gift cards, prepaid instruments, or other easily liquidated assets.

The primary objectives of churning fraud are to quickly monetize stolen card data before it is revoked, acquire goods or assets that can be anonymized or converted into cash with minimal traceability, and maximize financial gain from each compromised card before fraud controls or victims detect the activity.

name: Compromise Payment Gateway
description:
Fraudsters may gain unauthorized access to payment gateway platforms that process online transactions, allowing them to interfere with how payments are routed and recorded. Once embedded in a gateway environment, they can redirect transactions to accounts they control, alter transaction details to siphon funds, capture payment card and customer data, or disrupt normal settlement processes.

Compromise of a payment gateway can occur through exploitation of software vulnerabilities, use of stolen or weak credentials, phishing of gateway or merchant staff, or deployment of malware that intercepts traffic between merchants and the gateway. Fraud actors often focus on weaknesses in the integration between a merchant’s website and the gateway, or on misconfigurations and security gaps within the gateway’s own infrastructure, to maintain persistent and covert access.

name: Conversion to Physical Monetary Instruments
description: Fraud actors may turn digital or account‑based balances into physical money or negotiable instruments to complete cash‑out. By moving value into cash or cash‑like forms, they reduce traceability within electronic payment systems and gain flexibility to spend, transport, or further launder proceeds.

name: Conversion to Physical Monetary Instruments: Cash
description: Fraud actors may withdraw cash directly from compromised accounts using ATMs, in‑branch teller withdrawals, or cash‑back at point‑of‑sale. Cash withdrawals provide immediate access to funds and can be coordinated across multiple mules, cards, or locations to rapidly deplete balances before controls or fraud‑detection mechanisms respond.

name: Conversion to Physical Monetary Instruments: Cashier's Check
description: Fraud actors may request cashier’s checks funded from compromised accounts and payable to themselves, accomplices, or front entities. Once issued, cashier’s checks can be deposited, cashed, or used to purchase high‑value goods, providing a semi‑anonymous way to move and store value outside the original account.

name: Conversion to Physical Monetary Instruments: Money Order
description: Fraud actors may purchase money orders using funds drawn from compromised accounts, including via debit card, bank counter transactions, or other payment instruments. Money orders can then be cashed, resold, or used for payments (such as rent or goods), enabling further layering and obscuring the link to the original compromised account.

name: Convert to Cryptocurrency
description: Fraudsters may convert stolen or illicit funds into cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin or Ethereum to obscure the origin and movement of value. Cryptocurrency transfers leverage pseudonymous addresses and cross‑platform exchanges, making it more difficult for traditional financial monitoring and investigative processes to trace or recover the underlying funds.

name: Create Counterfeit Card
description: Fraudsters may manufacture physical payment cards using stolen or fabricated card data in order to conduct in‑person or card‑present transactions. This includes encoding compromised account details onto blank card stock or cloning existing cards so that fraudulent purchases, ATM withdrawals, or cash‑back transactions appear to originate from a legitimate debit or credit card.

name: Create Fake Materials
description: Fraud actors may create fraudulent materials to deceive victims or establish false legitimacy. This may include creating fake websites, fraudulent documents, counterfeit identification, or other materials designed to appear legitimate. Fake materials are used to support various fraud operations including phishing, identity fraud, business email compromise, or establishing fraudulent business entities.

name: Create Fake Materials: Fake Documents
description: Fraud actors may forge documents and supporting artifacts to falsify identities, deceive authorities, or fabricate evidence in support of fraud operations. This can include creating or altering identification cards, passports, financial statements, or shipping-related evidence such as tracking numbers to bypass verification processes, gain access to restricted services, or legitimize fraudulent transactions. Commonly faked documents include bank statements, paychecks, government-issued IDs, Social Security cards, insurance policies, invoices, business licenses, which may be either fully counterfeit or subtly modified to evade detection.

name: Create Fake Materials: Fake Website
description:
Fraud actors may create fraudulent e-commerce websites that mimic legitimate retailers to capture payment information or steal credentials. This may include replicating the design, layout, and functionality of trusted sites while hosting them on attacker-controlled infrastructure, often using lookalike domains (e.g., typosquatting) to appear legitimate. Fraud actors may advertise products with no intention of delivery to harvest payment card information during checkout.

Fraud actors may promote these sites through phishing campaigns, malicious advertisements, search engine optimization, or social media to drive victim traffic. Fraud actors use these sites to collect credentials, payment details, or personal data, redirect transactions, or facilitate additional fraudulent activity.

name: Create Fake Materials: Synthetic Media
description: Fraud actors may create or manipulate synthetic audio, video, images, or other media to impersonate a person, fabricate an identity, or support a fraudulent pretext. This may include deepfake video, generated identity images, cloned or altered voices, or real-time media manipulation. Fraud actors may use synthetic media to deceive victims and employees, bypass liveness or biometric verification, or convince targets to disclose information or authorize transactions.

name: Create Fake Materials: Spoofed Application
description: Fraud actors may create applications that mimic legitimate financial, investment, cryptocurrency, merchant, government, or service-provider applications. Spoofed applications may copy trusted branding, interfaces, workflows, and account information to deceive victims into entering credentials, payment data, personal information, or transferring funds. Fraud actors may distribute these applications through unofficial download sites, malicious links, third-party stores, or compromised accounts and may use them to support phishing, account takeover, or fraudulent investment schemes.

name: Open Financial Account
description:
Fraud actors may open financial accounts to establish actor-controlled infrastructure for receiving illicit funds or conducting fraudulent transactions. These accounts may be opened using the fraud actor’s own identity, stolen or synthetic identity information, fraudulent documents, shell businesses, front companies, or other misrepresentations intended to satisfy onboarding requirements.

Fraud actors may use these accounts to receive victim payments, deposit fraudulent instruments, transfer or cycle funds, make fraudulent purchases, process sham transactions, or withdraw funds before fraudulent activity is detected. The accounts may be opened at banks, credit unions, payment processors, financial technology services, or other institutions that hold or transfer funds.

name: Open Financial Account: Merchant Account
description:
Fraud actors may open merchant accounts with payment processors, acquiring banks, or other payment providers to obtain legitimate-appearing payment acceptance capabilities. These accounts may be opened using stolen or fabricated identity information, shell businesses, front companies, or falsified business documentation to bypass onboarding and identity-verification controls.

Fraud actors may use merchant accounts to receive payments for nonexistent or misrepresented goods and services, test payment cards at scale, process unauthorized transactions, or move and cycle illicit funds. By mimicking legitimate merchant activity, the accounts provide an actor-controlled point for receiving payments and disbursing proceeds while making transactions appear to originate from a legitimate business.

name: Open Financial Account: Consumer Account
description:
Fraud actors may open consumer financial accounts with the intention of receiving illicit funds or conducting fraudulent transactions. These accounts may be opened using the fraud actor’s own identity as part of first-party fraud or by using stolen, synthetic, or fabricated identity information. Opening an account commonly includes creating usernames, passwords, and other authentication credentials for the financial institution’s website or mobile application, allowing the fraud actor to access and manage the account remotely.

Fraud actors may use consumer accounts to receive victim payments, hold or transfer illicit proceeds, deposit fraudulent checks, make fraudulent purchases, or withdraw funds. For example, a fraud actor may open an account, deposit a bad check, and withdraw or spend the provisionally credited funds before the financial institution determines that the check is invalid.

name: Delete Relevant Emails
description: Fraudsters may delete emails that could alert victims or investigators to ongoing fraudulent activity. This can include removing copies of messages sent from the victim’s account, replies from recipients, security alerts about unusual login or transaction activity, or other notifications that would reveal account changes, preventing the legitimate user from noticing and responding to the compromise.

name: Device Fingerprint Spoofing
description: Fraud actors employ device fingerprint spoofing to mask their true identities and evade detection by security systems. By manipulating various attributes of their device's fingerprint, such as browser settings, operating system details, and hardware configurations, they can make their devices appear as different, legitimate ones. This technique enables fraud actors to bypass security measures that rely on device identification for authentication or fraud detection, allowing them to carry out illicit activities while remaining undetected.

name: Dispute Legitimate Transaction
description: Fraud Actors or complicit consumers may intentionally dispute legitimate card purchases or payment transactions to obtain unwarranted credits or refunds from a financial institution. By falsely claiming that a transaction was unauthorized, fraudulent, or that goods or services were not received, they seek to reverse charges while retaining the benefit of the original purchase.

name: Exploitation of Gambling Platforms
description:
Fraud actors may exploit gambling platforms as a channel to convert illicit value into seemingly legitimate funds and to move or disguise the proceeds of fraud. They may create or use accounts, often opened with stolen or fabricated identities, to deposit illicit funds, place low‑risk or offsetting bets, and then withdraw balances as “winnings” to other accounts under their control. They may also exploit bonus structures, loyalty rewards, or promotional credits to generate additional value, or conduct arbitrage across multiple platforms to turn promotional or gaming flows into profit. 

By routing funds through gambling platforms and generating complex patterns of bets, transfers, and payouts, actors aim to obscure the source of the money and make subsequent withdrawals appear consistent with normal gambling activity, supporting monetization and money‑laundering objectives rather than the initial execution of fraud.

name: Falsify Business Documents
description: Fraud actors may create or alter business documents to support fraud schemes or deceive stakeholders. This may include creating fake invoices, forging business licenses, falsifying financial statements, or creating fraudulent corporate documentation. Falsified documents may be used to establish fraudulent business entities, support business email compromise schemes, obtain financing, or deceive partners and customers.

name: Fraudulent Purchasing
description:
Fraudulent purchasing occurs when fraud actors use stolen payment card data, compromised or fraudulent accounts, or money laundering channels to buy goods or services. These purchases are used to convert illicit funds into seemingly legitimate assets, avoid scrutiny by financial institutions, or cash out stolen value into clean money.

Fraud actors may carry out fraudulent purchases using stolen credit card details or by abusing compromised financial accounts on e‑commerce platforms, payment processors (for example, gateway providers), or brick‑and‑mortar merchants with online payment capabilities. They may prioritize high‑value goods that can be quickly resold, or convert funds into cryptocurrencies or gift cards that provide liquid, harder‑to‑trace value.

Examples of fraudulent purchasing include: buying luxury items with stolen card information and reselling them for cash; ordering goods or services to drop addresses where they or associates can safely retrieve the items; and using illegitimately obtained funds to purchase gift cards or digital assets that have anonymous resale value or can be redeemed without exposing the buyer’s identity.

The primary objectives of fraudulent purchasing are to liquidate stolen financial assets before detection and account shutdown, launder money by transforming illicit funds into physical goods that can be resold for “clean” proceeds, and obtain goods or services for personal use or profit without any intention of legitimate payment.

name: Gather Customer Information
description:
Fraud actors may gather information about existing or prospective customers to support targeted fraud operations and social‑engineering attacks against financial institutions, merchants, or platforms. This can include collecting customer identity details (such as names, addresses, dates of birth, government identifiers), account and card data, contact information, relationship data (for example, employers, family members, or business associations), and behavioral or preference information (such as typical spending patterns or channel usage).

Customer information may be sourced from data breaches, underground markets, public records, social media, third‑party data brokers, compromised internal systems, or direct social‑engineering of customers and staff. Aggregated customer data enables more convincing impersonation, tailored fraud scenarios, and higher‑success attacks such as account takeover, new‑account fraud, mule recruitment, and highly targeted social‑engineering campaigns against both customers and the institutions that serve them.

name: Geolocation Spoofing
description: Fraud actors may falsify geographic location information to bypass location-based security controls or access restricted services. This may include using VPNs, proxy servers, GPS spoofing applications, or other techniques to mask true location. Location spoofing allows fraud actors to access geo-restricted content, bypass location-based fraud detection, or hide their true location during fraud operations.

name: Impersonate Account Holder
description: Fraud actors may impersonate legitimate account holders when interacting with financial institutions or service providers. This may include using stolen personal information to answer authentication questions, conducting social engineering attacks while impersonating victims, or using compromised identity information to convince institutions to grant access or conduct transactions. Successful impersonation can bypass identity verification controls.

name: Impersonate Official
description: Fraud actors may impersonate officials such as bank representatives, law enforcement officers, government agents, or other authority figures to manipulate victims. By impersonating officials, fraud actors leverage the trust and authority associated with these positions to convince victims to provide sensitive information, authorize transactions, or take actions that facilitate fraud. Impersonation may occur through phone calls, emails, or in-person interactions.

name: Insider Access Abuse
description: Fraud actors may abuse legitimate access privileges to conduct fraud operations. This may include malicious insiders, compromised insiders, or exploitation of excessive access privileges by authorized users. Insider access provides fraud actors with legitimate credentials and authorization to access systems, data, or conduct transactions, making detection more difficult than external attacks.

name: Interactive Voice Response Mapping
description: Fraud actors may interact with interactive voice response systems to understand call flows, authentication mechanisms, or available functions. By mapping IVR systems, fraud actors can identify opportunities for fraud, understand authentication requirements, or develop strategies for social engineering attacks against customer service representatives. IVR discovery may be automated or conducted manually to gather intelligence for fraud operations.

name: Mail Theft
description: Fraud actors may steal physical mail to obtain financial information, payment cards, checks, or identity documents. Mail theft provides access to statements, new payment cards, checks, tax documents, or other financial materials that can be used for fraud. Stolen mail may be intercepted from mailboxes, during postal delivery, or from mail processing facilities.

name: New Vendor Setup
description: Fraud actors may pretend to be a new vendor or supplier to trick organizations into directing payments to fraudulent accounts. New vendor setup can be initiated through fake invoices, requests for adding a new payee, banking information change forms, or urgent payment requests that pressure staff to bypass normal verification steps. Once the bogus vendor profile is established in accounts payable or procurement systems, fraud actors can submit additional invoices, alter payment details, or reroute legitimate payments intended for real vendors to accounts they control.

name: NFC Payment
description: Fraud actors exploit NFC (Near Field Communication) payments by using stolen or cloned NFC-enabled cards or mobile devices to make unauthorized transactions. They may intercept or manipulate NFC signals to initiate payments without the legitimate cardholder's knowledge or consent. By leveraging NFC technology, fraud actors can quickly and discreetly conduct fraudulent transactions, often evading traditional security measures such as PIN verification or signature requirements, leading to financial losses for both consumers and businesses.

name: PAN/CVV Generation
description: Fraud actors use PAN/CVV Generators to create valid credit card numbers (PANs) along with their corresponding Card Verification Values (CVVs), allowing fraud actors to bypass security measures and make unauthorized purchases. By generating PANs and CVVs, fraud actors can create counterfeit credit cards or conduct card-not-present transactions without physically possessing the victim's card.

name: PaReq Manipulation
description: Fraud actors exploit Payer Authentication Requests (PaReqs) by manipulating the data within these requests to bypass security measures and gain unauthorized access to sensitive information or transactions. By altering the parameters or contents of PaReqs, they can trick payment systems into approving fraudulent transactions without proper authentication. This manipulation helps fraud actors evade detection by exploiting vulnerabilities in payment processing systems and bypassing security checks designed to prevent unauthorized access or fraudulent transactions.

name: Phone Number Spoofing
description: Fraud actors may manipulate caller ID information so that outgoing calls appear to originate from a different phone number than the one actually used. This enables them to impersonate trusted organizations or ordinary customers in order to bypass call‑screening controls, establish credibility, and support social engineering or other fraudulent activity.

name: Phone Number Spoofing: Customer Phone Number Spoofing
description: Fraud actors may spoof a phone number that appears to belong to a legitimate customer or other ordinary individual when calling financial institutions or other official entities. By presenting themselves as the account holder from a plausible personal number, they attempt to pass identity verification, obtain confidential information about the customer, or convince staff to change account details, reset credentials, or otherwise grant access that facilitates downstream fraud like Impersonate Account Holder.

name: Phone Number Spoofing: Official Phone Number Spoofing
description: Fraud actors may spoof an official phone number associated with a trusted organization, such as a bank, government agency, or law enforcement office, when calling victims. By making the call appear to come from a recognized institution’s published number, they increase the likelihood that targets will trust the caller, disclose sensitive information, or perform high‑risk actions such as approving transactions or granting account access.

name: PIN-code Peeking
description:
Fraud actors observe or obtain personal identification numbers (PINs). Use of hidden cameras, skimming devices, or other covert methods to capture PINs at ATMs, point-of-sale terminals, or other PIN-entry locations.

Obtained PIN numbers used with other stolen information to compromise the victim's accounts or conduct fraudulent transactions.

name: Reactivate Account
description: Fraud actors target inactive bank accounts because they are less likely to be monitored closely by the account holder or financial institution. They may attempt to reactivate the bank account through social engineering or by exploiting loopholes in the bank's security procedures. Once reactivated, they can use the account to launder money, deposit counterfeit checks, or engage in other fraudulent activities, taking advantage of the perceived lack of scrutiny on inactive accounts.

name: Reversal of Transaction
description: Fraud actors exploit the Reversal of Operation by initially conducting a legitimate transaction, such as purchasing goods or services. After the transaction is complete and the funds have been transferred, they then reverse the transaction, claiming it was unauthorized or fraudulent. This technique may allow them to obtain the goods or services without actually paying for them, effectively evading detection and potentially causing financial loss to the legitimate party involved.

name: Scheduled Transfer
description:
Fraud actors use scheduled transfers to systematically move funds out of compromised accounts at predefined intervals. By creating or hijacking recurring payment instructions within online banking or payment services, they can quietly redirect money to accounts they control or to intermediaries that help conceal the origin of the funds.

Fraud actors may gain access to online banking or payment service accounts and configure new standing orders or modify existing ones to send funds to external destinations. These transfers are typically timed and sized to resemble normal business activity, helping them evade detection while routing money through shell entities, mule accounts, or cryptocurrency services as part of the laundering process.

name: Structuring
description: Fraud actors may structure transactions or account activity by breaking up large movements of funds, spreading activity across multiple accounts, or using different locations and channels to avoid triggering fraud controls and regulatory reporting thresholds. By parcelling deposits, withdrawals, or transfers into smaller amounts that fall below Currency Transaction Report (CTR) or Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) triggers, or by distributing activity over time and across institutions, they aim to keep illicit flows appearing routine and prevent automated systems or investigators from detecting the underlying money laundering or fraud.

name: Test Payment Thresholds
description: Fraud actors may perform small, low‑value “test” transactions to verify that stolen or compromised payment instruments can be successfully used before attempting larger fraud. In these tests, they confirm details such as whether the card or account is open, has not been blocked, passes authorization checks (for example, AVS/CVV or 3‑D Secure), and can complete online or card‑not‑present purchases without triggering strong controls. Successful tests indicate that a card or account is likely to support higher‑value charges or cash‑out attempts, allowing fraud actors to prioritize the most viable instruments for large‑scale fraudulent transactions or broader card‑testing campaigns.

name: Transfer of Funds
description:
Fraud actors may cause or facilitate the movement of funds from a victim or compromised account to an account, wallet, merchant, or other payment destination they control or can access through an intermediary. A transfer may be initiated without the account holder’s authorization or may be executed by a victim who has been deceived, coerced, or impersonated.

Fraud actors may use peer-to-peer payment services, real-time payment systems, regional payment rails, wire-transfer systems, cards, digital wallets, or other electronic mechanisms. They may route transfers through [money mules or mule-controlled accounts](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1049), shell entities, merchants, or multiple financial institutions to obtain usable value, distribute proceeds, cross jurisdictions, or make recovery and attribution more difficult.

name: Transfer of Funds: Peer-to-Peer Transfer
description:
Fraud actors may use peer-to-peer payment services to transfer funds between individuals, bank accounts, payment accounts, or digital wallets. These services commonly identify recipients through telephone numbers, email addresses, usernames, payment handles, or linked accounts and may make transferred funds available quickly.

Fraud actors may send funds from compromised accounts, deceive victims into sending payments, or route proceeds through mule-controlled peer-to-peer accounts. They may divide transfers among multiple recipient profiles or rapidly move received funds to other accounts or wallets to cash out, obscure control of the proceeds, or reduce the likelihood of recovery.

name: Transfer of Funds: Real-Time Payment
description:
Fraud actors may use real-time or instant payment systems to transfer funds within seconds or minutes, often at any time of day and with limited opportunity to stop or reverse the payment after it is accepted. These systems may support account-to-account transfers through banks, payment providers, or interoperable payment networks.

Fraud actors may initiate real-time payments from compromised accounts or deceive victims into authorizing payments to accounts controlled by the fraud actor, a money mule, or another intermediary. They may exploit the speed and finality of the payment to move funds onward through additional accounts or wallets, divide payments among multiple destinations, or withdraw or convert the funds before the victim or financial institution can intervene.

name: Transfer of Funds: Regional Payment Rail
description:
Fraud actors may use domestic or regional payment rails to transfer funds through clearing systems that support bank-to-bank credits and debits within a country or economic region. These mechanisms may include automated clearing house systems, Single Euro Payments Area credit transfers, and other local account-to-account networks.

Fraud actors may initiate individual, scheduled, repeated, or batched transfers to accounts controlled by themselves, money mules, or accomplices. They may use the broad availability, comparatively low transaction costs, processing windows, or settlement characteristics of these rails to move fraud proceeds at scale or make fraudulent transfers resemble routine payments.

name: Transfer of Funds: Wire Transfer
description:
Fraud actors may use domestic or international wire-transfer systems to move funds between financial institutions, including across jurisdictions. Wire transfers commonly support high-value transactions and may be difficult to reverse after the receiving institution makes the funds available.

Fraud actors may direct wire transfers to accounts controlled by themselves, money mules, shell companies, accomplices, or other intermediaries. They may divide or route funds through multiple institutions or jurisdictions, provide false payment purposes or beneficiary information, or quickly move received funds onward to hinder recovery and obscure beneficial ownership.

name: Use Virtual Cards
description:
Fraud actors use virtual cards to facilitate online fraud because they provide flexibility, anonymity, and rapid issuance for card‑not‑present transactions. Virtual cards are often obtained with weaker identity verification or sourced from compromised accounts, making them attractive instruments for testing stolen card data, funding mule accounts, or executing rapid series of purchases and refunds. Their disposability allows fraud actors to run multiple transactions, dispute or reverse charges, and then discard the card, reducing the risk that a single compromised instrument links together the broader scheme.

Virtual cards are frequently employed in promotion abuse, synthetic identity fraud, and account takeover scenarios, for example, to cash out loyalty points, rotate through trial or subscription offers, or route payments through intermediary wallets and marketplaces. They can also be used to create complex transaction chains across merchants and jurisdictions, complicating efforts to tie specific fraudulent purchases back to the originating compromised identity or account. This flexibility makes virtual cards a convenient tool for scaling and obscuring a wide range of digital fraud schemes, even when they are not explicitly part of a formal money‑laundering process.

name: Use Money Mule
description:
Fraud actors may use a money mule or mule-controlled account, card, wallet, payment instrument, identity, device, or business to receive, hold, transfer, withdraw, spend, transport, convert, or otherwise move fraud proceeds or fraudulently obtained assets. Mules may participate knowingly, remain willfully blind to the activity, or act without understanding that they are facilitating fraud.[[1]](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/common-frauds-and-scams/money-mules)

Fraud actors may direct mules to [open financial accounts](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1021), provide access to existing accounts, make [bank deposits](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1009) using fraudulent funds or instruments, receive payments from victims or other mules, conduct [transfers of funds](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1047) between accounts or wallets, purchase or exchange virtual currency, withdraw cash, or cash out compromised accounts.

Mules may also use compromised accounts or payment credentials to purchase goods, transport or deliver fraudulently obtained merchandise, resell goods, or return the resulting funds to the fraud actor.[[1]](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/common-frauds-and-scams/money-mules)[[2]](https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/ghost-tapping-chinese-criminal-ecosystem)

Fraud actors may use multiple mules or funnel accounts to aggregate funds, divide transactions, cross financial institutions or jurisdictions, and create distance between themselves and victims. Using these intermediaries can position funds for additional movement while obscuring the fraud actor’s identity, location, and control of the proceeds.

name: Operate Fraudulent Call Centers
description: Fraud actors may establish or operate coordinated call-center infrastructure to conduct fraud at scale. They may acquire phone systems, spoofed numbers, scripts, customer data, and teams of callers who impersonate trusted organizations or individuals. Centralized operations allow repeated voice phishing, account-recovery abuse, collection of credentials or one-time codes, and manipulation of victims into authorizing transactions.

name: Compromise Point-of-Sale Systems
description: Fraud actors may compromise point-of-sale terminals to capture payment data, manipulate transactions, or obtain unauthorized funds. Compromise may involve exploiting software vulnerabilities, installing malware, altering terminal configuration, connecting unauthorized hardware, or abusing remote administration access. Fraud actors may use the compromised system to collect card data and PINs, redirect payments, issue fraudulent refunds, or conceal unauthorized transactions.

name: Clone Victim Device
description:
Fraud actors may clone a cellular phone by reprogramming another handset to transmit the subscriber identifiers assigned to a legitimate device. In legacy cellular systems, these identifiers may include the electronic serial number (ESN), mobile identification number (MIN), and system identification number (SID). Fraud actors may obtain valid identifier combinations by unlawfully monitoring radio transmissions or through other compromised sources.

When the legitimate and cloned phones transmit the same identifiers, the cellular network may be unable to distinguish between them. This may allow fraud actors to obtain unauthorized telecommunications access, place calls, or incur charges that are billed to the legitimate subscriber. This technique is specific to cloning a cellular device’s network identity and is distinct from Device Fingerprint Spoofing, which manipulates device characteristics evaluated by fraud-detection systems.

name: Search Dark Web
description: Fraud actors may search dark-web marketplaces, access-controlled forums, leak sites, criminal communities, or other non-public online sources for information that can support fraud. They may look for exposed credentials, payment data, customer records, organization details, vulnerabilities, access offers, or operational guidance. Information gathered from dark-web sources may be used to identify targets, select an initial access vector, purchase supporting resources, or tailor follow-on social-engineering and account-takeover activity.

name: Impersonate Trusted Person
description: Fraud actors may impersonate a person that a victim knows or trusts, such as a co-worker, family member, or business partner. They may use email, messaging, phone calls, social media, or other communication channels to make requests appear legitimate. By exploiting an existing relationship, fraud actors may convince victims to disclose information, change payment details, approve access, or perform fraudulent transactions.

name: Payment via Gift Card
description: Fraud actors may obtain or direct payment through physical or digital gift cards to receive, transfer, or launder money. They may use stolen funds to purchase gift cards, coerce victims to provide gift-card numbers or redemption codes, or move value through gift-card exchanges and resale markets. Gift cards can provide rapid settlement, broad availability, and reduced linkage to traditional bank accounts, allowing fraud actors to spend or resell the value while obscuring the original source of funds.

name: Train AI Model
description: Fraud actors may train, fine-tune, prompt, or otherwise configure artificial intelligence models to support fraud operations. They may use stolen data, synthetic identities, impersonation scripts, target-specific information, or prior victim interactions to improve model outputs. Trained models may generate convincing messages and media, automate interactive conversations, adapt social-engineering pretexts, or scale fraud activity across many targets and communication channels.

name: Coercion
description: Fraud actors may pressure, threaten, manipulate, or otherwise coerce a victim into taking an action that supports fraud. They may create urgency, claim that funds or accounts are at risk, invoke authority, threaten financial or personal consequences, or maintain prolonged psychological pressure. Coercion may position the victim to disclose information, change account settings, grant access, or execute transactions, and may continue while the fraudulent action is performed.

name: Create Online Persona
description:
Fraud actors may create and cultivate online personas to support fraud operations. An online persona may be fictitious, impersonate a real person or organization, or combine real and fabricated information. Persona development may include creating a believable identity, establishing an online presence and history, adding profile information and images, developing relationships or affiliations, and maintaining consistent activity across one or more online services.

Fraud actors may use online personas to identify and approach potential victims, establish trust, support impersonation or social engineering pretexts, promote fraudulent investments or services, distribute phishing content, or direct victims into subsequent fraud activity. A persona may be maintained on a single platform or coordinated across multiple platforms to make the identity appear established and legitimate.

name: Create Online Persona: Dating App Account
description:
Fraud actors may create and cultivate accounts on dating applications or relationship-oriented services to establish an online persona and build trust with potential victims. Accounts may contain fabricated or stolen biographical details, photographs, employment information, interests, and other content intended to make the persona appear legitimate.

Fraud actors may maintain conversations and simulated relationships over time before introducing fraudulent requests or directing victims to other communication channels. Dating app personas may support romance scams, fraudulent investment schemes, requests for money or gifts, collection of credentials or personal information, or other fraud activity.

name: Create Online Persona: Social Media Account
description:
Fraud actors may create and cultivate social media accounts to build online personas that support targeting and fraud operations. These personas may be fictitious, impersonate real people or organizations, or combine real and fabricated information. Persona development may include completing profile information, adding photographs, establishing a posting history, developing social connections, and presenting affiliations that make the account appear legitimate.

Fraud actors may maintain personas on one social media service or coordinate them across multiple services. They may use these accounts to identify and connect with targets directly or through existing relationships, establish credibility, impersonate trusted parties, distribute phishing or scam content, promote fraudulent investments or services, and move victims into subsequent fraud activity.

name: Establish Relationships
description:
Fraud actors may establish relationships with individuals to develop the trust, familiarity, or emotional connections needed to facilitate fraudulent activity. They may engage in repeated interactions, express shared interests, offer companionship or support, or otherwise cultivate a relationship that appears genuine.

Fraud actors may maintain these relationships over extended periods to establish credibility, gain influence, and increase an individual’s receptiveness to future requests or financial exploitation. This behavior is commonly used in romance scams, pig-butchering investment scams, advance-fee schemes, and other confidence-based fraud. For example, a fraud actor may develop a friendship before promoting a fraudulent investment, requesting money, collecting sensitive information, or inducing another action that supports fraud.

name: Establish Relationships: Romantic Relationship
description:
Fraud actors may foster a real or perceived romantic or intimate relationship to develop emotional trust, attachment, or dependence. They may express romantic interest, affection, or commitment and engage in repeated personal interactions intended to make the relationship appear genuine.

Fraud actors may cultivate the relationship over an extended period to gain influence and exploit the individual’s emotional connection. Romantic relationships are commonly cultivated during romance scams and may also form the trust-building component of pig-butchering schemes. Fraud actors may use this influence to solicit money, promote fraudulent investments, obtain sensitive information, or induce other actions that facilitate fraud.

name: Establish Relationships: Social Relationship
description:
Fraud actors may cultivate a friendship or other non-romantic personal relationship through shared interests, companionship, support, or regular social interaction. These interactions may be used to develop personal trust, familiarity, or an emotional connection that makes the relationship appear genuine.

Fraud actors may use the resulting influence to encourage fraudulent investments, solicit money, obtain personally identifiable information or financial-account details, or induce other actions that facilitate fraud. For example, a fraud actor conducting a pig-butchering scheme may develop a friendship through repeated conversations before introducing a fraudulent investment opportunity.

name: Establish Relationships: Professional Relationship
description:
Fraud actors may establish professional or business relationships to develop credibility, trust, influence, or access. They may present themselves as potential business partners, colleagues, clients, advisors, vendors, recruiters, or collaborators and engage in interactions that appear to serve a legitimate professional purpose.

Fraud actors may use these relationships to obtain sensitive information, influence business or financial decisions, solicit fraudulent investments or payments, gain access to organizations or accounts, or induce individuals to perform other actions that facilitate fraud. These relationships may support fraudulent investment, employment, procurement, or business-opportunity schemes.

name: Sale of Securities
description:
Fraud actors may sell securities associated with fraudulent activity to convert the holdings into funds or other readily usable value.

Fraud actors may liquidate securities obtained through stolen funds, unauthorized account access, deceptive transactions, or other fraudulent means. They may dispose of holdings after manipulating their price, trading volume, or perceived demand through [Manipulation of Securities](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1063), or sell securities before related manipulation, misrepresentation, or account compromise is discovered.

Fraud actors may route sales through multiple accounts, brokers, intermediaries, or controlled entities to obscure beneficial ownership or the source of the holdings. They may use the proceeds to realize profits, transfer or launder value, distribute gains among participants, or complete a securities fraud scheme while attempting to avoid detection or regulatory scrutiny.

name: Manipulation of Securities
description:
Fraud actors may manipulate the price, market value, trading volume, or perceived supply or demand of a security by artificially increasing or decreasing those indicators to create favorable conditions for fraud or financial gain.

Fraud actors may disseminate false or misleading information, fabricate investment analysis or endorsements, promote or disparage a security, or manipulate market sentiment through social media, messaging platforms, investment forums, and other communication channels. They may coordinate purchases or sales, conduct trades between controlled accounts, place or cancel orders, or use other trading activity to create the appearance of rising or falling demand, liquidity, price movement, or legitimate investor interest.

Fraud actors may use the manipulated conditions to attract or deter investors, induce victims to buy, hold, or sell the security, increase or decrease the apparent value of existing holdings, profit from long or short positions, or support other fraudulent representations. Related to [Sale of Securities](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1062), they may sell holdings at an artificially elevated price, profit from a decline, or acquire securities at an artificially depressed price.

name: Exploit Transaction Processing Gaps
description:
Fraud actors may exploit gaps or timing differences in how financial transactions are authorized, posted, made available, settled, reconciled, or reversed to obtain or move value before an institution fully validates the transaction.

Fraud actors may take advantage of provisional credit, delayed check clearing, offline or batch processing, inconsistent controls across channels, or synchronization failures between systems. They may deposit a fraudulent or unfunded instrument and withdraw or transfer provisionally available funds before the item is returned, move unsettled funds between linked accounts or products, or conduct withdrawals or internal transfers while an ATM or payment network is offline.

Fraud actors may repeat or coordinate transactions across accounts, channels, or institutions to increase the amount obtained and cash out before the processing gap is detected or corrected. They may use the resulting funds for purchases, transfers, cash withdrawals, or other activities that realize value from the exploited gap.

name: Create Synthetic Identity
description:
Fraud actors may create a synthetic identity by combining fabricated identity attributes with authentic, stolen, or otherwise misused personally identifiable information. Unlike impersonation of a specific individual, a synthetic identity represents a constructed persona that may not correspond to any single real person.

Fraud actors may combine names, dates of birth, government-issued identifiers, addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses, photographs, or other identity attributes to make a synthetic identity appear legitimate. They may reuse attributes across multiple synthetic identities or create slight variations of the same identity to evade identity-linkage and duplicate-identity controls.

Fraud actors may create supporting documents, contact information, devices, online activity, financial records, or credit history to increase the apparent legitimacy of a synthetic identity and improve its ability to pass identity-proofing and onboarding controls. They may cultivate the identity over time before using it to [open financial accounts](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1021), obtain credit, or facilitate other fraudulent activity.

Accounts established with synthetic identities may subsequently be used to receive or conduct [transfers of funds](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1047), support [money-mule activity](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1049), build credit before a bust-out, or facilitate laundering and other fraud schemes.

name: Bypass Controls
description:
Fraud actors may bypass controls by causing a security, identity-verification, authentication, authorization, risk-scoring, transaction-monitoring, or fraud-prevention mechanism not to evaluate, challenge, block, or flag fraudulent activity. The defining behavior is the deliberate avoidance of a control’s decision or enforcement point, independent of the specific fraudulent action that follows.

Fraud actors may select a channel, workflow, account feature, or transaction path where a control is absent or applied less rigorously; invoke an exception, fallback, recovery, or manual-review process; manipulate inputs or contextual data used by rules or risk models; or rely on a legitimate identity, trusted account status, customer classification, or established history to avoid step-up verification. These approaches allow fraudulent activity to proceed through otherwise legitimate processes without triggering the safeguards that would normally interrupt or surface it.

name: Mule Recruitment
description:
Fraud actors may recruit individuals to serve as money mules by persuading, deceiving, compensating, or coercing them into providing accounts, payment instruments, identities, or labor for a fraud scheme. Recruited individuals may knowingly participate, disregard indications of criminal activity, or remain unaware that they are facilitating fraud.[[1]](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/common-frauds-and-scams/money-mules)

Fraud actors may approach prospective mules through fraudulent employment opportunities, romance or investment schemes, advance-fee scams, social media messages, direct personal contact, or advertisements on criminal forums and messaging platforms. They may offer commissions, reimbursements, travel, or other compensation; exploit an established relationship; present a false explanation for the requested activity; or use pressure, threats, or coercion. Criminal organizations may also use mule controllers, handlers, or previously recruited mules to identify, recruit, and manage additional participants. Criminal syndicates have used Telegram-based marketplaces to recruit mules for ATM withdrawals, fraudulent purchases, transportation, resale, and money laundering roles.[[2]](https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/ghost-tapping-chinese-criminal-ecosystem)

Recruitment may occur immediately before the requested activity. For example, a fraud actor may approach an individual at an ATM, present a fabricated reason that the actor cannot use their own account, and persuade the individual to deposit a check and return the provisionally available funds. The subsequent use of the individual or their financial resources is covered by [Use Money Mule](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1049).

name: Call Forwarding
description:
Fraud actors may enable call forwarding on a victim’s telephone number to redirect some or all incoming calls to an actor-controlled destination. They may deceive the victim into dialing a service code or entering a sequence of numbers by presenting it as a verification step, security procedure, or customer-service instruction.

Fraud actors may use redirected calls to intercept authentication or account-recovery communications, receive calls from financial institutions or service providers, impersonate the victim, or prevent the victim from receiving fraud alerts. Because the victim may retain outgoing calling and other telephone services, the forwarding may not be immediately apparent.

name: Phishing
description:
Fraud actors may use deceptive communications to socially engineer victims into disclosing sensitive information or performing actions that enable unauthorized access or other fraudulent activity. Phishing may target a particular individual or organization or may be conducted through broadly distributed campaigns.

Fraud actors may pose as [trusted friends, relatives, colleagues, or other people](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1056) or [banks, government agencies, merchants, or other official organizations](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1032), [disguise the source of an email](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/T1672) or [make a telephone call appear to come from a trusted number](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1040), use compromised accounts or existing message threads, and create urgency or alarm to make their communications appear legitimate. They may request credentials, one-time passcodes, payment information, personal information, account details, or security answers. Fraud actors may also direct victims to [fraudulent websites](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1020.002) or actor-controlled telephone numbers, induce them to install [fraudulent applications](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1020.004) or [remote-access software](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/T1219), approve [authentication requests generated by the fraud actor](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/T1621), authorize malicious applications, or [change account or security settings](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1005).

name: Phishing: Vishing
description:
Fraud actors may use telephone calls, voicemail, or other voice communications to socially engineer victims into disclosing sensitive information or performing actions that facilitate unauthorized access or other fraudulent activity. This form of voice phishing is commonly known as vishing.

Fraud actors may pose as [trusted friends, relatives, colleagues, or other people](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1056) or [financial institutions, government agencies, employers, merchants, and other official organizations](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1032). They may request credentials, one-time passcodes, payment information, account details, security answers, or personal information. They may also direct victims to visit a [fraudulent website](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1020.002), install a [fraudulent application](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1020.004) or [remote-access software](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/T1219), approve an authentication request, change a security setting, or call an actor-controlled number. Fraud actors may [make calls appear to originate from an official telephone number](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1040.002) to make the communication appear legitimate. Vishing may be conducted manually, through [fraudulent call centers](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1050) or robocalls, or with [altered or synthetically generated voices](https://ctid.mitre.org/fightfraud#/technique/F1020.003).

name: Phishing: Smishing
description:
Fraud actors may use SMS, MMS, or other mobile text-messaging services to socially engineer victims into disclosing sensitive information or performing actions that facilitate unauthorized access or other fraudulent activity. This form of text-message phishing is commonly known as smishing.
